Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Rise along the left leg to the apex, descend the right leg, then attach a crossbar between two interior sites.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw one stem through its midpoint, then return through the upper and lower curved bowls.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Make one open curved return from the upper right to the lower right; the two ends remain distinct.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw a straight stem, lift, then attach a curved return from its top to its bottom.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw a stem through the middle attachment, then add the top, middle, and bottom bars.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw a stem through the middle attachment, then add a bar at its top and another at its midpoint.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Follow an open curved return, rise a short distance at its lower end, then turn inward.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw two stems, each with an interior site, then draw a bridge between those two sites.
Corpus.Note: The bridge is drawn left-to-right here. That is historical order, not a one-way traffic law.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw a top bar, attach a central stem, then draw a bottom bar through its lower endpoint.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw a top bar, then descend from its right end and curve left into an open hook.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw the stem, then descend from the upper right into its midpoint and leave toward the lower right.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Descend the stem and continue around the bottom corner without lifting the pen.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Rise, descend toward an interior valley, rise again, and descend the opposite side in one continuous path.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Rise on the left, descend diagonally to the lower right, then rise on the right.
Corpus.Note: Its distinction from Z depends on the selected horizontal and vertical frame.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Traverse a rounded closed contour and return to the actual starting site.
Corpus.Note: Four native quadratic sections provide one rounded outline; this is not an exact metric-circle claim.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw a stem, then add a curved return from its top to an interior site, leaving a lower tail.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw a closed rounded contour, lift, then draw a short diagonal across its lower right area.
Corpus.Note: The tail is a separate stroke with separate sites. A visible intersection does not silently weld it to the contour.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw a stem and upper bowl, then add a diagonal leg from their shared interior junction.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Follow an upper curved return into a middle site, then reverse the bending sense through the lower return.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw the top bar through its central site, lift, then attach a descending stem to that site.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Descend the left side, follow a curved bottom return, and rise on the right without lifting.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Descend to one bottom site, then rise from that same site toward the opposite upper end.
Corpus.Note: A low point is not, by itself, a certificate of physical instability; that needs a support and load context.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Descend, rise to an inner peak, descend again, then rise to the final endpoint.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw two diagonals, lifting between them. Their central sites coincide in this view but are independently identified.
Corpus.Note: This is a crossing interpretation. See the joined variant for an explicit four-arm shared site.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Descend from the upper left through a junction into the stem, lift, then attach the upper right arm.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Cross the top, descend diagonally to the lower left, then cross the bottom in one path.
Corpus.Note: Rotate its viewing frame and the same unlabelled three-link topology admits another glyph interpretation.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Traverse one rounded closed contour; no topology-only read distinguishes this fixture from O.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Draw a short leading diagonal into the top of a stem, descend, then add a baseline through its bottom site.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Curve across the top, descend diagonally to the lower left, then turn along the baseline.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Make two successive rightward curved returns joined at a middle site, with no stem closing either bowl.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Descend diagonally, turn right through a crossing site, then lift and draw a stem through that site.
Corpus.Note: This open-top 4 has no cycle. The closed-top variant shares the upper starting site and does have one.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Cross the top toward the left, descend a short stem, then make a curved lower return.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Curve down from a free upper tail into a bowl, then travel around that bowl back to its actual joining site.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Cross the top and descend diagonally from its right endpoint without lifting.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Trace an upper loop, return to the waist, then trace a lower loop through the same waist.

Corpus.Title: One supplied construction
Corpus.Construction: Trace an upper loop and continue from its joining site into a descending curved tail.

Corpus.Title: Stem plus attached foot
Corpus.Construction: Draw the stem, lift, then attach the foot at its lower endpoint.
Corpus.Note: Same actual sections and sites as the baseline. Only the selected ordered construction history changes; no traffic permission is implied.

Corpus.Title: Continuous top corner
Corpus.Construction: Start at the top bar's right end, turn down into the whole stem, then add the middle bar.
Corpus.Note: Same actual sections and sites as the baseline. Only the selected ordered construction history changes; no traffic permission is implied.

Corpus.Title: Opposed bridge read
Corpus.Construction: Draw the same two stems, then draw the bridge from right to left.
Corpus.Note: Same actual sections and sites as the baseline. Only the selected ordered construction history changes; no traffic permission is implied.

Corpus.Title: Two corner traversals
Corpus.Construction: Turn from the left arm down the stem, lift, retrace that same stem upward, then turn onto the right arm.
Corpus.Note: Same actual sections and sites as the baseline. Only the selected ordered construction history changes; no traffic permission is implied.

Corpus.Title: Outward construction read
Corpus.Construction: Rise through the stem and leave along the left arm, then draw the right arm outward from the junction.
Corpus.Note: Same actual sections and sites as the baseline. Only the selected ordered construction history changes; no traffic permission is implied.

Corpus.Title: Two legs plus crossbar
Corpus.Construction: Draw the left leg to the apex, lift and draw the right leg down, then attach the crossbar.
Corpus.Note: Same actual sections and sites as the baseline. Only the selected ordered construction history changes; no traffic permission is implied.

Corpus.Title: Two separately traced loops
Corpus.Construction: Complete the upper loop, lift, then complete the lower loop through the same actual waist.
Corpus.Note: Same actual sections and sites as the baseline. Only the selected ordered construction history changes; no traffic permission is implied.

Corpus.Title: Continuous stem and return
Corpus.Construction: Rise along the stem and continue around the curved return to close in one stroke.
Corpus.Note: Same actual sections and sites as the baseline. Only the selected ordered construction history changes; no traffic permission is implied.

Corpus.Title: Bars before stem
Corpus.Construction: Draw the three bars first, then connect their left sites with the stem.
Corpus.Note: Same actual sections and sites as the baseline. Only the selected ordered construction history changes; no traffic permission is implied.

Corpus.Title: Four-arm shared junction
Corpus.Construction: Draw two diagonals through one explicitly shared central site.
Corpus.Note: The silhouette matches the crossing fixture, but the selected incidence graph has one component and a degree-four junction. Flow routes are still a separate question.

Corpus.Title: Closed-top construction
Corpus.Construction: Join the diagonal and vertical strokes at their upper endpoint, creating a triangular cycle.
Corpus.Note: This changes the actual topology, unlike merely changing pen order.

Cases.Title: L as a continuous bend
Cases.Construction: Draw the stem and continue around the corner without lifting.
Cases.Use: A stream can follow the explicit turn.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: One packet follows the declared turn from the top through the corner to the right.
The same visible bend does not imply a reverse route. That closed law admits no return.

Cases.Title: Attached corner, use unresolved
Cases.Construction: Draw the stem, lift, then attach the arm at the same site.
Cases.Use: The pieces are joined, but the passage rule has not been supplied.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: Two strokes meet at a shared site, but the use law is open. Attachment is known; passage is not.

Cases.Title: Attached corner with passage
Cases.Construction: Draw the stem, lift, then attach the arm at the same site.
Cases.Use: A stream can follow the explicit turn.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: An explicit passage makes the separately attached pieces behave like the continuous bend for this input.

Cases.Title: T as a terminal
Cases.Construction: The stem reaches a shared crossbar site.
Cases.Use: A load or message can arrive without permission to leave through either arm.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: The empty closed law blocks the packet, which remains at its source.

Cases.Title: T as a through path with an unused stem
Cases.Construction: The bar is drawn continuously; the stem is attached later.
Cases.Use: The bar can carry a stream while the stem remains an unselected possibility.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: The legal horizontal route crosses the branch site without turning.
A geometric T does not grant its stem an outgoing route.

Cases.Title: T as an unresolved choice
Cases.Construction: Three arms share a site.
Cases.Use: Two legal outlets are alternatives for one packet, not copies of it.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: Both alternatives are preserved. No packet moves until a choice is supplied.

Cases.Title: T as a controlled switch
Cases.Construction: Three arms share a site; a separate control is connected to the permission law.
Cases.Use: The control selects an outlet while the other outlet remains physically present.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: The selected control admits only the left outlet.

Cases.Title: T switch with uncertain control
Cases.Construction: Three arms share a site; a separate control is connected to the permission law.
Cases.Use: The control selects an outlet while the other outlet remains physically present.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: The control could select either side. The packet stays owned once at the source.

Cases.Title: T switch with an open control read
Cases.Construction: Three arms share a site; a separate control is connected to the permission law.
Cases.Use: The control selects an outlet while the other outlet remains physically present.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: A known left possibility plus an open tail does not justify committing to left.

Cases.Title: T with uncertain permission to move
Cases.Construction: The stem can reach the right arm through a control-gated passage.
Cases.Use: An uncertain control can mean move or hold, even when only one route is visible in the candidate union.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: There is only one candidate route, but one possible control blocks it. The packet cannot move yet.
Both remaining controls permit the same route. This coarser action is certain even though the control is not.

Cases.Title: T as a material merge
Cases.Construction: The two arms and stem share one junction; two inlet routes point to one receiver.
Cases.Use: The shared receiver limits the combined input. Material identity is retained, unlike a Boolean OR read.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: Two independent packets enter one receiver with two sites. Both identities survive the merge.

Cases.Title: T merge with insufficient capacity
Cases.Construction: The two arms and stem share one junction; two inlet routes point to one receiver.
Cases.Use: The shared receiver limits the combined input. Material identity is retained, unlike a Boolean OR read.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: One receiving site cannot hold two packets. The atomic batch is refused; neither packet is lost.

Cases.Title: H as a one-way bridge
Cases.Construction: Draw two separate stems, then connect their intermediate sites with a bar.
Cases.Use: Connection is structural; direction of permitted use is an additional relation.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: The crossbar connects the stems and permits left-to-right passage.
Drawing a connector, or calling it a bridge, does not supply its return route.

Cases.Title: H as a two-way bridge
Cases.Construction: Draw two separate stems, then connect their intermediate sites with a bar.
Cases.Use: Connection is structural; direction of permitted use is an additional relation.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: One packet crosses the explicit forward route.
The same packet returns through a separately encoded reverse route.

Cases.Title: Cross as independent passages
Cases.Construction: Two strokes have coincident middle coordinates but different actual sites.
Cases.Use: Geometric intersection does not create a material connection.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: Two streams cross in the drawing but use separate middle sites and never exchange.

Cases.Title: Cross as a shared turning junction
Cases.Construction: The horizontal and vertical strokes share their actual middle site.
Cases.Use: A connected turning route changes the output direction.
Cases.Limits: This fixture demonstrates connected permissions and packet accounting. It does not infer handwriting, mechanical stiffness, timing, or a physical load law from the outline.

Probes.Explanation: A genuinely shared site plus an explicit turning route lets the west stream leave north.

Cases.Title: A: between two feet
Cases.Construction: Two legs end on the declared ground; the crossbar is a separate attachment.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: A: move the load, keep the letter
Cases.Interpretation: The same support no longer brackets the supplied load.
Cases.Construction: Only the query location changes; the source shape and contacts are retained.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: V: a single contact
Cases.Interpretation: A pivot or funnel is a plausible use; broad support is not supplied.
Cases.Construction: Both arms meet at one actual site on the ground.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: V: a small off-centre demand
Cases.Interpretation: A single contact does not bracket an offset load.
Cases.Construction: One contact stays fixed while the selected load position changes.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: Invert V: now two ground contacts
Cases.Interpretation: The same path topology can serve as a two-legged support candidate.
Cases.Construction: Reverse its vertical placement and declare the two lower endpoints as contacts.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: N: two feet, without a baseline bar
Cases.Interpretation: Bracing is a possible use, but the diagonal is not a material-strength proof.
Cases.Construction: A continuous path visits both lower sites; they are explicitly chosen as contacts.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: Z: a baseline bar
Cases.Interpretation: This coarse contact read agrees with N, despite the different baseline structure.
Cases.Construction: The bar's endpoints are declared contacts. No continuous contact pressure distribution is inferred.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: Z: change the supporting frame
Cases.Interpretation: Ground is contextual: this read uses a vertical wall as its reference.
Cases.Construction: Choose the left two endpoints and project across onto the wall instead of down onto a floor.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: T: a post and a top surface
Cases.Interpretation: A central pedestal needs additional support assumptions.
Cases.Construction: The top and stem share an actual midpoint; the only declared floor contact is the post foot.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: H: two posts joined across
Cases.Interpretation: A bridge or brace candidate with two supports.
Cases.Construction: The crosspiece shares both mid-stem sites. A contact-span read says nothing about traversal permission.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: A: the contacts were not supplied
Cases.Interpretation: A familiar outline is insufficient to answer this support query.
Cases.Construction: The source shape remains present; the selected contact inventory is empty.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Cases.Title: A: the contact inventory is incomplete
Cases.Interpretation: A partial read must not confidently report outside the support.
Cases.Construction: One contact is supplied in an open inventory; other contacts remain unspecified.
Cases.Limits: Projection relative to selected contacts only; no rigidity, forces, friction or dynamic stability law is supplied.

Transfers.Name: Bend
Transfers.Glyphs: L, U, V, corners of Z
Transfers.Structure: An ordered handoff between two incident sections.
Transfers.Use: Continue a cursor or packet around a change of heading.
Transfers.Needs: A connected continuation route; history alone does not install it.
Transfers.Limit: Does not establish a rigid joint, strength, or two-way traffic.

Transfers.Name: Attachment
Transfers.Structure: A later element shares an existing endpoint or interior site.
Transfers.Use: Add a branch, handle, joist, sensor or sign without replacing the carrier.
Transfers.Needs: Shared site plus a selected coupling or route, if interaction is intended.
Transfers.Limit: An attachment does not automatically give all incident paths permission to communicate.

Transfers.Name: Bridge
Transfers.Structure: Two distinct local sites are joined by a third section.
Transfers.Use: Exchange across previously separate strands or support a transverse span.
Transfers.Needs: Separate directional permissions, capacity and receiver availability for material exchange.
Transfers.Limit: One drawn bridge does not imply two-way use, simultaneous use or mechanical load bearing.

Transfers.Name: Choice
Transfers.Structure: One arrival can address several possible continuations.
Transfers.Use: Select an outlet according to a control or retain unresolved alternatives.
Transfers.Needs: A finite law and a rule for actual acceptance; uncertain prediction must not copy a packet.
Transfers.Limit: A visual fork does not choose, prioritize or duplicate by itself.

Transfers.Name: Merge
Transfers.Glyphs: Y, junctions of M and W
Transfers.Structure: Several source routes meet one receiving site or passage.
Transfers.Use: Combine observations, or compete for a material receiver.
Transfers.Needs: An observation OR law or an explicit conserving transfer; these are different uses.
Transfers.Limit: Participation OR is not addition of conserved material.

Transfers.Name: Crossover
Transfers.Structure: Two visible paths can coincide in projection while their sites remain distinct.
Transfers.Use: Pass independently, or install an explicit exchange junction as an alternative.
Transfers.Needs: Actual identity/coupling evidence; crossing ink is not enough.
Transfers.Limit: The drawing cannot decide over/under, contact or weld.

Transfers.Name: Enclosure
Transfers.Structure: Selected connected sections contain graph cycles.
Transfers.Use: A loop, feedback route, container boundary or repeated circuit can be proposed.
Transfers.Needs: A planar boundary read for area; a directed route and controller for recurrent execution.
Transfers.Limit: An undirected graph cycle proves neither enclosed physical volume nor a running feedback loop.

Transfers.Name: Support and range
Transfers.Glyphs: A, H, N, V, Z, T
Transfers.Structure: A projected query lies between, on or outside selected contacts.
Transfers.Use: A support-span check, bracketed estimate or between-anchors query.
Transfers.Needs: Declared frame, contacts and projection; material mechanics need further laws.
Transfers.Limit: No stiffness, mass distribution, friction, force balance or statics is solved here.

Transfers.Name: Surface for activity
Transfers.Structure: A crosspiece exposes locations for additional relations.
Transfers.Use: A workspace, exchange surface or display arrangement can attach to those sites.
Transfers.Needs: The interacting participants, goals, actions and histories must be connected in the relevant context.
Transfers.Limit: A table-shaped graph does not encode eating, paperwork, gambling or linguistic meanings by itself.

Limits: These are authored constructions and contextual probes, not learned semantic categories.
Contact-span inclusion is one geometric condition, not certification of stability. N and Z can agree under this coarse read.
The local words count a shared uncalibrated reach. The renderer supplies pixels; no physical unit or universal glyph proportion is inferred.
The native read is observational. It does not mutate the glyph, apply a force, or settle a mechanical structure.
